claim: During the preparation of a saccadic eye movement, human observers anticipate defining features of the eye movement target in pre-saccadic foveal vision.
source: We previously demonstrated that during the preparation of a saccadic eye movement, human observers anticipate defining features of the eye movement target in pre-saccadic foveal vision (Kroell and Rolfs, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Kroell and Rolfs, 2022).

claim: The conspicuity of feature information at the saccade target location influences the magnitude and time course of foveal enhancement.
source: In this Research Advance, we show that the conspicuity of feature information at the saccade target location influences the magnitude and time course of foveal enhancement.
evidence: This is the main finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: An increase in opacity from 25% to 90% translated to an increase in luminance contrast from 0.53 to 0.78 (Michelson contrast).
source: An increase in target opacity from 25% to 90% corresponded to an increase in Michelson, 1927 from 0.53 to 0.78 and an increase in the SNR of the filtered orientation from 1.40 to 2.58 (see Methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements and calculations described in the Methods section.

claim: An increase in opacity from 25% to 90% translated to an increase in signal-to-noise ratio of orientation information from 1.40 to 2.58.
source: An increase in target opacity from 25% to 90% corresponded to an increase in Michelson, 1927 from 0.53 to 0.78 and an increase in the SNR of the filtered orientation from 1.40 to 2.58 (see Methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements and calculations described in the Methods section.

claim: Foveal enhancement defined as the difference between hit rates to target-congruent and target-incongruent foveal probes increased with target opacity.
source: Foveal enhancement defined as the difference between hit rates to target-congruent and target-incongruent foveal probes increased with target opacity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: The time course of foveal enhancement showed an oscillatory pattern that was particularly pronounced at high target opacities.
source: Moreover, the time course of foveal enhancement showed an oscillatory pattern that was particularly pronounced at high target opacities.
evidence: This finding is supported by time-resolved data analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: At higher target opacities, false alarms were increasingly triggered by signal, i.e., by incidental orientation information in the foveal noise.
source: Reverse correlations furthermore suggest that at higher target opacities, false alarms were increasingly triggered by signal, i.e., by incidental orientation information in the foveal noise.
evidence: This claim is supported by reverse correlation analysis of false alarm trials.

claim: Presenting the saccade target at a high signal-to-noise ratio appears beneficial, as foveal congruency effects, especially when time-resolved, are most robustly detectable.
source: Presenting the saccade target at a high signal-to-noise ratio appears beneficial, as foveal congruency effects, especially when time-resolved, are most robustly detectable.
evidence: This is a practical recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Starting 175 ms before saccade onset, observers' hit rates for foveal probes with target-congruent orientation significantly exceeded incongruent hit rates.
source: Starting 175 ms before saccade onset, observers' hit rates (HRs) for foveal probes with target-congruent orientation significantly exceeded incongruent HRs.
evidence: This is a finding from the previous study (Kroell and Rolfs, 2022) cited in the Introduction.

claim: The congruency effect was spatially confined to the center of gaze and its immediate vicinity.
source: This congruency effect was spatially confined to the center of gaze and its immediate vicinity and more pronounced during saccade preparation than during passive fixation.
evidence: This is a finding from the previous study cited in the Introduction.

claim: The congruency effect was more pronounced during saccade preparation than during passive fixation.
source: This congruency effect was spatially confined to the center of gaze and its immediate vicinity and more pronounced during saccade preparation than during passive fixation.
evidence: This is a finding from the previous study cited in the Introduction.

claim: Feedback connections from higher-order visual areas enhance relevant saccade target features in foveal retinotopic cortex.
source: Based on these findings, we proposed that feedback connections from higher-order visual areas enhance relevant saccade target features in foveal retinotopic cortex (see also Williams et al., 2008; Chambers et al., 2013; Fan et al., 2016; Weldon et al., 2016; Yu and Shim, 2016; Weldon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by the authors' previous findings and other cited studies.

claim: Internal orientation predictions combine with feedforward foveal input to early visual cortex and facilitate the detection of target-congruent feature information in the center of gaze.
source: Internal orientation predictions subsequently combine with feedforward foveal input to early visual cortex and facilitate the detection of target-congruent feature information in the center of gaze.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism based on the authors' findings.

claim: Neuronal response latencies decrease systematically as the contrast of visual input increases.
source: In particular, neuronal response latencies decrease systematically as the contrast of visual input increases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about visual processing.

claim: The phenomenon of contrast-dependent latency decrease is reliably observed at varying stages of the visual processing hierarchy—such as the lateral geniculate nucleus, primary visual cortex, and anterior superior temporal sulcus.
source: While this phenomenon is reliably observed at varying stages of the visual processing hierarchy—such as the lateral geniculate nucleus (Lee et al., 1981), primary visual cortex (e.g. Albrecht, 1995; Carandini and Heeger, 1994; Carandini et al., 1997; Carandini et al., 2002), and anterior superior temporal sulcus (STSa; Oram et al., 2003; van Rossum et al., 2008)—influences of contrast on neuronal response latency are particularly pronounced in higher-order visual areas
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: Influences of contrast on neuronal response latency are particularly pronounced in higher-order visual areas.
source: While this phenomenon is reliably observed at varying stages of the visual processing hierarchy—such as the lateral geniculate nucleus (Lee et al., 1981), primary visual cortex (e.g. Albrecht, 1995; Carandini and Heeger, 1994; Carandini et al., 1997; Carandini et al., 2002), and anterior superior temporal sulcus (STSa; Oram et al., 2003; van Rossum et al., 2008)—influences of contrast on neuronal response latency are particularly pronounced in higher-order visual areas
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: A doubling of stimulus contrast decreases the latency of V1 neurons by 8 ms.
source: a doubling of stimulus contrast has been shown to decrease the latency of V1 neurons by 8 ms, compared to a reduction of 33 ms in area STSa (Oram et al., 2003; van Rossum et al., 2008).
evidence: This specific quantitative finding is supported by citations.

claim: A doubling of stimulus contrast decreases the latency of area STSa neurons by 33 ms.
source: a doubling of stimulus contrast has been shown to decrease the latency of V1 neurons by 8 ms, compared to a reduction of 33 ms in area STSa (Oram et al., 2003; van Rossum et al., 2008).
evidence: This specific quantitative finding is supported by citations.

claim: Both congruent and incongruent hit rates decreased with increasing target opacity.
source: Both congruent and incongruent HRs decreased with increasing target opacity (Figure 2A, left panel), arguably because attentional resources were increasingly drawn to the target the more salient it became.
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The decrease in foveal hit rates with increasing target opacity was less pronounced for probes with target-congruent orientation than for incongruent probes.
source: This decrease in foveal HRs, however, was less pronounced for probes with target-congruent orientation (slope of the linear regression line: –0.46% [congruent] vs –1.73% [incongruent] per opacity step, p<0.001).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: In all four opacity conditions, observers detected foveal probes more readily if they exhibited the same orientation as the saccade target.
source: In all four opacity conditions, observers detected foveal probes more readily if they exhibited the same orientation as the saccade target, resulting in significantly higher congruent as compared to incongruent HRs (HRcong-incong=3.3%, 3.4%, 5.4–6.8%, ps<0.021; Figure 2A, middle panel).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The fixed effect of target opacity on enhancement in hit rates reached significance (t(34) = 2.341, p=0.025).
source: The fixed effect of target opacity reached significance, t(34) = 2.341, p=0.025.
evidence: This is a result from the linear mixed-effects model analysis.

claim: As the opacity of the saccade target increased, the difference between hit rates for target-congruent and target-incongruent foveal probes increased.
source: More specifically, as the opacity of the saccade target increased, the difference between HRs for target-congruent and target-incongruent foveal probes increased as well, resulting in a significantly positive slope of the fitted linear regression line (slope = 1.3% per opacity step, p<0.001; Figure 2A, right panel).
evidence: This finding is supported by regression analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: On probe-absent trials, observers reported perceiving the target orientation more often than the non-target orientation for the 25%, 59%, and 90% opacity conditions.
source: On probe-absent trials, observers reported perceiving the target orientation more often than the non-target orientation for the 25%, 59%, and 90% opacity conditions, resulting in significantly higher congruent as compared to incongruent false alarm rates (FARs; FARcong-incong=6.5%, 6.2, and 4.6%, ps<0.02; Figure 2B).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The fixed effect of target opacity did not affect the differences in false alarm rates (t(34) = –0.44, p=0.661).
source: Unlike for HRs, the fixed effect of target opacity did not affect the differences in FARs, t(34) = –0.44, p=0.661.
evidence: This is a result from the linear mixed-effects model analysis.

claim: The slope of the fitted linear regression line for the difference in false alarm rates was statistically indistinguishable from zero (–0.2% per opacity step, p=0.713).
source: The slope of the fitted linear regression line was statistically indistinguishable from zero (–0.2% per opacity step, p=0.713).
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis.

claim: Congruent and incongruent false alarm rates both decreased with increasing target opacity.
source: Inspecting congruent and incongruent FARs instead of their difference revealed that, just like HRs, they both decreased with increasing target opacity.
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The decrease in false alarm rates with increasing target opacity was comparable for congruent and incongruent false alarms (slopes: –1.9% vs –1.6% per opacity step, p=0.715).
source: This decrease, however, was comparable for congruent and incongruent FARs (slopes: –1.9% vs –1.6% per opacity step, p=0.715).
evidence: This finding is based on statistical comparison of regression slopes.

claim: The difference in filter energies around the target and non-target orientation was significantly more pronounced for the higher as compared to the lower two target opacities (p=0.008).
source: Interestingly, the difference in filter energies around the target and non-target orientation was significantly more pronounced for the higher as compared to the lower two target opacities (p=0.008; Figure 2C).
evidence: This finding is based on reverse correlation analysis and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The contribution of 'true Hits' to the pool of foveal false alarms increased with target opacity.
source: This observation suggests that the contribution of 'true Hits' to the pool of foveal FAs increased with target opacity, allowing systematic orientation effects to manifest in average noise properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reverse correlation analysis.

claim: There was a moderate yet nonsignificant negative correlation (r=–0.41, p=0.278) between the z-standardized slope of the difference in hit rates and the z-standardized slope of the difference in false alarm rates.
source: This analysis yielded a moderate yet nonsignificant negative correlation between HR and FAR slopes (r=–0.41, p=0.278).
evidence: This is a result from correlation analysis.

claim: Observers who showed more enhancement in hit rates as target opacity increased tended to show a smaller difference between congruent and incongruent false alarm rates with increasing opacity.
source: In other words, observers who showed more enhancement in HRs as target opacity increased tended to show a smaller difference between congruent and incongruent FARs with increasing opacity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis result.

claim: Higher target opacity levels increased observers' sensitivity for congruent foveal orientation signals.
source: Nonetheless, it suggests that higher target opacity levels increased observers' sensitivity for congruent foveal orientation signals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation analysis and reverse correlation findings.

claim: Median saccade latencies decreased as the opacity and contrast of the saccade target increased (median mdn = 288.8, 279.7, 276.4, and 268.0 ms).
source: Median saccade latencies decreased as the opacity and, therefore, the contrast of the saccade target increased (median mdn = 288.8, 279.7, 276.4, and 268.0 ms; Figure 3A).
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of saccade latency data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The slope of the linear regression line fitted to median latencies on an individual-observer level was significantly smaller than zero (mean m=–6.57 ms/opacity step, p<0.001).
source: The slope of the linear regression line fitted to median latencies on an individual-observer level was significantly smaller than zero (mean m=–6.57 ms/opacity step, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a result from regression analysis of saccade latency data.

claim: Target opacity did not affect the precision of saccadic timing.
source: Target opacity did not affect the precision of saccadic timing: the slope of the regression line fitted to the standard deviation of latencies on an individual-observer level was not significantly smaller than zero (m=–0.41 ms/opacity step, p=0.169).
evidence: This finding is based on statistical analysis of saccade latency variability.

claim: The center of mass of saccade landing coordinates fell inside the target region in all opacity conditions.
source: The center of mass fell inside the target region in all conditions, demonstrating that observers were able to execute accurate saccades even at the lowest opacity.
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of saccade landing positions.

claim: Saccade amplitudes were uninfluenced by target opacity (mdn = 10.20, 10.31, 10.25, and 10.33 dva).
source: Indeed, saccade amplitudes were uninfluenced by target opacity (mdn = 10.20, 10.31, 10.25, and 10.33 dva): the slope of the regression line fitted to median amplitudes on an individual-observer level was statistically indistinguishable from zero (m=0.03 dva/opacity step, p=0.153, Appendix 1—figure 1D, panel 2).
evidence: This finding is based on statistical analysis of saccade amplitude data.

claim: Saccadic error defined as the Euclidean distance between saccade landing coordinates and the center of the target stimulus did not vary with target opacity (mdn = 1.35, 1.35, 1.38, and 1.37 dva, p=0.171).
source: Likewise, saccadic error defined as the Euclidean distance between saccade landing coordinates and the center of the target stimulus did not vary with target opacity (mdn = 1.35, 1.35, 1.38, and 1.37 dva, p=0.171; Appendix 1—figure 1D, panel 3).
evidence: This finding is based on statistical analysis of saccade accuracy data.

claim: Saccadic peak velocities decreased significantly with opacity (mdn = 416.7, 413.70, 410.17, 407.25 dva/s, p<0.001).
source: Saccadic peak velocities, on the other hand, decreased significantly with opacity (mdn = 416.7, 413.70, 410.17, 407.25 dva/s, p<0.001; Appendix 1—figure 1D, panel 4).
evidence: This finding is based on statistical analysis of saccade velocity data.

claim: The main sequence defined as the relation between saccade amplitudes and peak velocities remained largely unaltered across opacity conditions.
source: However, due to the small absolute scale of these variations, the main sequence defined as the relation between saccade amplitudes and peak velocities remained largely unaltered (Appendix 1—figure 1C).
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of the relationship between saccade amplitude and velocity.

claim: For targets with 59% opacity, congruent hit rates significantly exceeded incongruent ones if the probe appeared 100–150 or 200–300 ms after the target (p=0.003 and p<0.001).
source: For targets with 59% opacity, congruent HRs significantly exceeded incongruent ones if the probe appeared 100–150 or 200–300 ms after the target (p=0.003 and p<0.001).
evidence: This finding is based on time-resolved analysis of hit rates.

claim: For the highest target opacity, a continuous enhancement window was observed ranging from 100 to 200 ms after target onset (ps<0.003).
source: For the highest target opacity, we observed a continuous enhancement window ranging from 100 to 200 ms after target onset (ps<0.003).
evidence: This finding is based on time-resolved analysis of hit rates.

claim: At an opacity of 39%, significant enhancement manifested during the 50 ms immediately preceding saccade onset (p=0.006).
source: At an opacity of 39%, significant enhancement manifested during the 50 ms immediately preceding saccade onset, p=0.006.
evidence: This finding is based on saccade-locked time-resolved analysis.

claim: As target opacity increased, enhancement was additionally observable in an earlier saccade preparation bin from 150 to 100 ms before eye movement onset (p=0.003).
source: As target opacity increased further, enhancement was additionally observable in an earlier saccade preparation bin from 150 to 100 ms before eye movement onset, p=0.003.
evidence: This finding is based on saccade-locked time-resolved analysis.

claim: At the highest target opacity, congruent hit rates exceeded incongruent ones in the 150–100 ms bin exclusively (p=0.005).
source: At the highest target opacity, congruent HRs exceeded incongruent ones in the 150–100 ms bin exclusively, p=0.005.
evidence: This finding is based on saccade-locked time-resolved analysis.

claim: Foveal enhancement is observable in earlier stages of saccade preparation as target opacity increases.
source: In short, the corrected saccade-locked time courses appear to suggest that foveal enhancement is observable in earlier stages of saccade preparation as target opacity increases.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the corrected time-course analysis.

claim: The average foveal enhancement across target opacities reached significance starting 115 ms before saccade onset (all ps<0.046).
source: The average foveal enhancement across target opacities reached significance starting 115 ms before saccade onset (gray curve in Figure 4; all ps<0.046).
evidence: This finding is based on continuous time-course analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: For every individual target opacity condition, significant enhancement was observed immediately before saccade onset.
source: For every individual target opacity condition, we observed significant enhancement immediately before saccade onset, although only very briefly for the lowest opacity (−2 to 0 ms for 25%; –39 to 0 ms for 39%, –106 to 0 ms for 59%, and –13 to 0 ms for 90%; all ps<0.050; yellow to dark red curves in the first row of Figure 4).
evidence: This finding is based on continuous time-course analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: For the higher two target opacities, a local maximum in enhancement was observed preceding eye movement onset by approximately 80 ms.
source: Especially for the higher two target opacities, we observed a local maximum preceding eye movement onset by approximately 80 ms.
evidence: This observation is based on inspection of the continuous time-course data.

claim: Peaks in enhancement relied on both oscillatory increases in congruent hit rates and simultaneous decreases in incongruent hit rates.
source: Peaks in enhancement relied on both oscillatory increases in congruent HRs and simultaneous decreases in incongruent HRs.
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of congruent and incongruent hit rates separately.

claim: Enhancement peaks appear to reflect a foveal enhancement of target-congruent feature information along with a concurrent suppression of target-incongruent features.
source: In other words, enhancement peaks appear to reflect a foveal enhancement of target-congruent feature information along with a concurrent suppression of target-incongruent features.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pattern observed in congruent and incongruent hit rates.

claim: All previously described effects were amplified in the subset of short-latency saccades.
source: All previously described effects were amplified in the subset of short-latency saccades (mean n=1623 trials per observer): across all time points, the difference between congruent and incongruent HRs reached significance for target opacities ≥ 39% and increased with opacity (slope = 2.85% per opacity step, p<0.001; Figure 5A).
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of trials split by saccade latency.

claim: For short-latency saccades, the difference between congruent and incongruent hit rates reached significance for target opacities ≥ 39% and increased with opacity (slope = 2.85% per opacity step, p<0.001).
source: across all time points, the difference between congruent and incongruent HRs reached significance for target opacities ≥ 39% and increased with opacity (slope = 2.85% per opacity step, p<0.001; Figure 5A).
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of short-latency saccade trials.

claim: For short-latency saccades, the difference in false alarm rates did not vary significantly with opacity (slope = 0.64% per opacity step, p=0.883).
source: The difference in FARs, in turn, did not vary significantly with opacity (slope = 0.64% per opacity step, p=0.883).
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of short-latency saccade trials.

claim: For short-latency saccades, there was a moderately negative yet nonsignificant correlation of r=–0.49 (p=0.181) between the normalized differences in hit rates and false alarm rates.
source: Again, we observed a moderately negative yet nonsignificant correlation of r=–0.49 (p=0.181) between the normalized differences in HRs and FARs.
evidence: This is a result from correlation analysis of short-latency trials.

claim: Long-latency saccades showed a markedly different pattern: enhancement in hit rates was overall less pronounced and even decreased with increasing target signal-to-noise ratio (slope = –1.23% per SNR step, p=0.044).
source: Long-latency saccades, in contrast, showed a markedly different pattern (mean n=1218 trials per observer): enhancement in HRs was overall less pronounced and even decreased with increasing target SNR (slope = –1.23% per SNR step, p=0.044; Figure 5B).
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of long-latency saccade trials.

claim: For long-latency saccades, the differences in hit rates and false alarm rates were entirely uncorrelated (r=0.09, p=0.823).
source: The differences in HRs and FARs were entirely uncorrelated (r=0.09, p=0.823).
evidence: This is a result from correlation analysis of long-latency trials.

claim: Short-latency saccades, which were enabled by effective attentional target selection and oculomotor planning, had driven the enhancement effects reported for the entire trial pool.
source: These findings suggest that short-latency saccades, which were enabled by effective attentional target selection and oculomotor planning, had driven the enhancement effects reported for the entire trial pool (see Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of short- and long-latency saccade results.

claim: The small but significant decrease in enhancement with increasing target opacity in the long-latency subset could suggest that long-latency saccades to high-contrast targets in particular rely on attentional lapses.
source: The small but significant decrease in enhancement with increasing target opacity in the long-latency subset could suggest that long-latency saccades to high-contrast targets in particular rely on attentional lapses, which affected pre-saccadic perceptual processes as well as oculomotor behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the long-latency saccade results.

claim: The manipulation of target opacity influenced saccade metrics: saccade latencies, as well as saccadic peak velocities, decreased with increasing opacity.
source: First, the manipulation of target opacity influenced saccade metrics: saccade latencies, as well as saccadic peak velocities, decreased with increasing opacity.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the Results section.

claim: The decrease in saccade latencies with increasing target opacity likely reflects a facilitation of movement planning toward high-contrast target stimuli.
source: The decrease in latencies was to be expected and likely reflects a facilitation of movement planning toward high-contrast target stimuli (Ludwig et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The small yet significant decrease in peak velocities with increasing target opacity was unexpected and has not been observed previously.
source: The small yet significant decrease in peak velocities, which cannot be explained by a concomitant decrease in saccade amplitudes, was unexpected and, to our knowledge, has not been observed previously.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: Higher peak velocities may serve to compensate for longer saccade latencies by slightly decreasing the overall time interval between target appearance and saccade landing.
source: Hypothetically, higher peak velocities may serve to compensate for longer saccade latencies by slightly decreasing the overall time interval between target appearance and saccade landing.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis to explain the peak velocity finding.

claim: Hit rates for target-congruent and -incongruent foveal probes decreased as target opacity increased, likely because attention was increasingly drawn to the target the more salient it became.
source: Second, HRs for target-congruent and -incongruent foveal probes decreased as target opacity increased, likely because attention was increasingly drawn to the target the more salient it became.
evidence: This is a summary finding with an inferential explanation.

claim: Presenting the target at a high opacity (59% and above) seems beneficial since congruency effects, especially when time-resolved, are more robustly detectable.
source: From an experimenter's perspective, presenting the target at a high opacity (59% and above in our design) seems beneficial since congruency effects, especially when time-resolved, are more robustly detectable.
evidence: This is a practical recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Pre-saccadic attention seems to select the target orientation in an automatic fashion, even when the eye movement could easily be programmed based on local contrast variations alone.
source: On a more conceptual level, pre-saccadic attention seems to select the target orientation in an automatic fashion, even when the eye movement could easily be programmed based on local contrast variations alone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that enhancement occurs even at high target opacities.

claim: The influence of peripheral orientation information on foveal detection judgments is directly proportional to the strength of the orientation signal at the target location.
source: The influence of peripheral orientation information on foveal detection judgments is directly proportional to the strength of the orientation signal at the target location.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding regarding the relationship between target opacity and enhancement.

claim: Saccades are routinely directed toward the currently most conspicuous object in the scene during spontaneous eye movement behavior.
source: As during spontaneous eye movement behavior, saccades are routinely directed toward the currently most conspicuous object in the scene ('t Hart et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about natural viewing behavior supported by citation.

claim: The finding that enhancement increases with target conspicuity underscores the feasibility of predictive foveal processing in natural visual environments.
source: This finding underscores the feasibility of predictive foveal processing in natural visual environments.
evidence: This is an inference about the ecological relevance of the findings.

claim: The relation between target opacity and foveal enhancement was exclusively driven by saccades with latencies below an observer's median latency in each opacity condition.
source: Of note, the relation between target opacity and foveal enhancement was exclusively driven by saccades with latencies below an observer's median latency in each opacity condition.
evidence: This is a summary of the saccade latency analysis results.

claim: Short saccade latencies reflect effective target selection and oculomotor planning, which in turn benefits pre-saccadic perceptual processes such as foveal prediction.
source: we suggest that short saccade latencies reflect effective target selection and oculomotor planning, which in turn benefits pre-saccadic perceptual processes such as foveal prediction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects observed for short vs. long latency saccades.

claim: When systematic variations of saccade latency were taken into account, congruent and incongruent hit rates differed earlier for higher target opacities.
source: Third, target opacity influenced the time course of enhancement in HRs. When systematic variations of saccade latency were taken into account (Figure 3B, third row), congruent and incongruent HRs differed earlier for higher target opacities.
evidence: This is a summary of the time-course analysis results.

claim: The feedforward processing of the peripheral saccade target may have been accelerated when it was presented at high contrast.
source: These findings suggest that the feedforward processing of the peripheral saccade target may have been accelerated when it was presented at high contrast (Albrecht et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the time-course effects, supported by citation.

claim: Weaker feedforward signals may require a longer accumulation interval before the feedback process can be initiated.
source: Alternatively, or in addition, it is conceivable that weaker feedforward signals require a longer accumulation interval before the feedback process can be initiated.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the time-course effects.

claim: Foveal congruency effects appear to exhibit an oscillatory pattern, with peaks in a medium saccade preparation stage (~80 ms before the eye movement) and immediately before saccade onset.
source: Moreover, foveal congruency effects appear to exhibit an oscillatory pattern, with peaks in a medium saccade preparation stage (~80 ms before the eye movement) and immediately before saccade onset.
evidence: This is a summary of the oscillatory pattern observed in the time-course data.

claim: Unlike rapid feedforward processing, feedback propagation has been shown to follow an oscillatory rhythm in the alpha and beta range, i.e., between 7 and 30 Hz.
source: Unlike rapid feedforward processing, feedback propagation has been shown to follow an oscillatory rhythm in the alpha and beta range, i.e., between 7 and 30 Hz (Bastos et al., 2015; Jensen et al., 2015; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about feedback processing supported by citations.

claim: It is possible that the object-processing areas that send feedback to retinotopic visual cortex do so at a temporal frequency of ~12.5 Hz.
source: In our case, it is possible that the object-processing areas that send feedback to retinotopic visual cortex do so at a temporal frequency of ~12.5 Hz.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism underlying the oscillatory pattern.

claim: At higher stimulus contrasts, feedforward signals may be fed back instantaneously and without the need for signal accumulation in feedback-generating areas.
source: At higher stimulus contrasts, feedforward signals may be fed back instantaneously and without the need for signal accumulation in feedback-generating areas.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about why oscillations are more prominent at higher contrasts.

claim: Perceptual and attentional processes have been shown to exhibit oscillatory modulations that are phase-locked to action onset.
source: In accordance with this, perceptual and attentional processes have been shown to exhibit oscillatory modulations that are phase-locked to action onset (e.g. Tomassini et al., 2015; Hogendoorn, 2016; Wutz et al., 2016; Benedetto and Morrone, 2017; Tomassini et al., 2017; Benedetto et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Task-induced cognitive influences are not the only possible explanation for the considerable variability in temporal characteristics of foveal feedback during passive fixation.
source: task-induced cognitive influences suggested to underlie the considerable variability in temporal characteristics of foveal feedback during passive fixation (e.g. Fan et al., 2016; Weldon et al., 2016; Weldon et al., 2020) are not the only possible explanation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and previous literature.

claim: Low-level target properties such as luminance contrast modulate the time course of foveal feedback and should be equally considered.

Despite this spatial unpredictability, however, congruency effects peaked at the pre-saccadic foveal location, even after peripheral baseline performances had been raised to a foveal level through an adaptive increase in probe opacity.

In particular, the thalamic pulvinar has been identified as a connection hub for visual processing that receives copies of feedforward and feedback connections from different visual areas and may even combine information across visual space (Cortes et al., 2024).
